MeSH Keywords: Humans, Down Syndrome, Neurons, Brain, Signal Transduction, Hypoxia-Inducible Factor 1


--- ABSTRACT ---
Down syndrome (DS) is the most frequently diagnosed chromosomal disorder of chromosome 21 (HSA21) aneuploidy, characterized by intellectual disability and reduced lifespan. The transcription repressor, Repressor Element-1 Silencing Transcription factor (REST), which acts as an epigenetic regulator, is a crucial regulator of neuronal and glial gene expression. In this study, we identified and investigated the role of REST-target genes in human brain tissues, cerebral organoids, and neural cells in Down syndrome. Gene expression datasets generated from healthy controls and DS samples of human brain tissues, cerebral organoids, NPC, neurons, and astrocytes were retrieved from the Gene Ontology (GEO) and Sequence Read Archive (SRA) databases. Differential expression analysis was performed on all datasets to produce differential expression genes (DEGs) between DS and control groups. REST-targeted DEGs were subjected to functional ontologies, pathways, and network analyses. We found that REST-targeted DEGs in DS were enriched for the JAK-STAT and HIF-1 signaling pathways across multiple distinct brain regions, ages, and neural cell types. We also identified REST-targeted DEGs involved in nervous system development, cell differentiation, fatty acid metabolism and inflammation in the DS brain. Based on the findings, we propose REST as the critical regulator and a promising therapeutic target to modulate homeostatic gene expression in the DS brain.

key_findings.finding: Direct REST/NRSF evidence is strongest for lithium: in rat embryonic neural stem cells, lithium increased neuronal differentiation and reduced ethanol-induced NRSF/REST protein abundance and DNA-binding activity (PMID 18671961). This is mechanistic and direct, but it is an injury/interference model rather than a genome-wide lithium signature study.

The key convergent mood-stabilizer signature paper (PMID 25451397) used a 90-plus-gene qPCR array in human SH-SY5Y neuroblastoma cells after 1-hour lithium or sodium valproate exposure. Nine genes were significantly regulated overall: DRD3, FOS, JUN, GAD1, NRG1, PAFAH1B3, PER3, RELN and RGS4; FOS/JUN implicated AP-1, and transcriptional-network enrichment of the regulated set identified NRSF/REST as an important upstream regulatory mechanism. This is indirect/convergent evidence: NRSF was inferred by enrichment, not measured as REST expression, occupancy, binding, or protein activity.

key_findings.finding: A broader SH-SY5Y Affymetrix microarray study of 1 mM lithium chloride or sodium valproate for 6 or 72 hours reported 936 statistically significant expression changes, with Six1 showing a maximum 31.3-fold induction and protein-level validation; the mechanistic follow-up linked Six1, not REST, to anti-apoptotic protection. REST/NRSF was not reported as a measured driver in the abstract, so this provides broad convergent transcriptomic evidence for shared lithium/valproate responses but no direct REST attribution.

key_findings.finding: All four drugs show a shared astrocytic transcriptomic response, but it is not REST-specific: in human U-87 MG astrocyte-derived cells treated with lithium, valproic acid, carbamazepine, and lamotrigine, microarray analysis found FEZ1 as the only commonly induced gene; induction was validated at transcript and protein levels. The study did not report REST/NRSF expression, binding, or REST-target gene-set enrichment. Thus, this is convergent across drugs at FEZ1, not evidence that REST mediates the common signature.

key_findings.finding: For lamotrigine, a primary rat hippocampal-cell cDNA array after 0.1 mM for one week found eight genes upregulated and six downregulated; GABA-A receptor beta3 was validated by Northern blot and in situ hybridization in CA1, CA3, and dentate gyrus. No REST/NRSF measurement or REST-target enrichment was reported, so evidence is currently absent for direct REST involvement.

key_findings.finding: REST-regulated neuronal programs are biologically plausible downstream comparators: independent REST datasets associate REST targets with synaptic function, ion-channel conductivity, vesicular transport, neuronal development, and—in human Down-syndrome brain/neural-cell datasets—JAK-STAT and HIF-1 signaling, plus inflammation and fatty-acid metabolism. However, these are REST biology reference gene sets, not evidence that mood stabilizers induce or repress them.

key_findings.finding: Overall conclusion: lithium has one direct mechanistic REST/NRSF link and one indirect transcriptomic-enrichment link; valproate shares the indirect NRSF-enrichment signal with lithium but lacks direct REST validation; carbamazepine and lamotrigine have no convincing direct or gene-set-level REST evidence in the retrieved literature. Convergence across all four drugs is demonstrated for FEZ1 in astrocytes, not for REST-regulated genes/pathways.
